the adjusted odds ratio point estimate is 1.204, 95% CI [0.997,1.453], p=0.053
after adjustment, the odds of a red card are 20.4% higher for dark-skinned players, but the CI includes 1.0 so it is not significant at 0.05
the unit of analysis was the player-referee dyad
the analysis included 99,645 player-referee dyads
there were 1,214 unique players, 1,123 light-skinned and 236 dark-skinned
there were 2,978 unique referees
light-skinned dyads numbered 83,655 with 1,016 red cards, a 1.21% rate
dark-skinned dyads numbered 15,990 with 225 red cards, a 1.41% rate
skin tone was measured as the average of two independent raters' assessments on a 5-point scale from 0 (very light) to 1 (very dark)
inter-rater reliability was Pearson r=0.923, described as excellent agreement
light skin was defined as an average rating ≤0.25
dark skin was defined as an average rating ≥0.75
medium skin tones (0.25-0.75) were excluded from the primary binary comparison
the model included log-transformed number of games in the dyad as an exposure covariate
the model included a 12-category position covariate with Attacking Midfielder as reference
the model included a 4-category league-country covariate with England as reference
the model included player height (continuous) as a covariate
the model included player weight (continuous) as a covariate
46,383 dyads (31.8% of the original 146,028) were excluded in total
21,407 dyads (14.7%) were excluded for lacking a skin tone rating (players without photos)
17,015 dyads (11.7%) were excluded for having medium skin tone
7,961 dyads (5.4%) were excluded for missing covariates, primarily missing position (7,471)
logistic regression was used as the model
the outcome was a binary indicator of any red card in the dyad versus none
standard errors were clustered at the player level since each player appears in about 80 dyads
risk difference was estimated via predictive margins/G-computation, setting all observations to dark vs light skin and averaging
confidence intervals came from a parametric bootstrap with 10,000 draws from the multivariate normal distribution of parameter estimates
the p-value was a two-sided test based on the proportion of simulated risk differences ≤0
the hypothesis that referees give more red cards to dark-skinned players is not supported by the analysis
the adjusted risk difference is not statistically significant at α=0.05, since p=0.051 exceeds threshold and the CI includes zero
despite being called "marginally significant" by some, the conventional threshold was not met and the null hypothesis cannot be rejected under the requested two-sided α=0.05 framework
the absolute effect size is small: baseline risk 1.21% for light-skinned vs estimated 1.45% for dark-skinned, a 0.24 pp increase
the difference represents a 20% relative increase in red-card risk
given the rarity of red cards and potential measurement error, this small effect is difficult to distinguish from noise
the effect varies dramatically by league, confirmed by an interaction test (χ²(3)=22.24, p<0.001)
adjusted odds ratios by league were Germany 2.00, England 1.48, Spain 0.98, France 0.75
the heterogeneity suggests the relationship is context-dependent, driven mainly by England/Germany, undermining generalizability of the overall estimate

spans.assertion: the evidence for the hypothesis is at best marginal and inconsistent, though point estimates consistently suggest a small positive association
the association does not reach conventional statistical significance (p=0.051)
the confidence interval includes zero
there is substantial heterogeneity across contexts
the absolute effect size is very small (0.24 pp)

spans.note: May be subject to unmeasured confounding

spans.assertion: the analysis does not provide convincing evidence that referees systematically discriminate against dark-skinned players; p=0.051 means data this extreme would occur ~5.1% of the time under no true effect
the substantial league variation suggests any bias is highly context-dependent, and the protective effect in France plus null effect in Spain contradict a simple discrimination narrative

spans.note: Offers speculative, unconfirmed explanations for the heterogeneity (racial composition, referee training, playing styles, chance variation)

spans.assertion: even accepting the point estimate, the effect is small: it implies dark-skinned red card probability rising from 1.21% to 1.45%, i.e. 1-2 additional red cards in a ~300-game season

spans.note: Any bias is ethically concerning but magnitude is subtle and hard to attribute definitively

spans.assertion: given marginal evidence, heterogeneity, small effect size, and potential confounding, the analyst concludes the hypothesis is NOT SUPPORTED
